analysis.one_liner: Freezes large agribusiness, food manufacturing, and grocery mergers while a commission studies food-industry concentration.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to two House committees in September 2018 and got no vote or hearing before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned mergers between large agribusinesses, food and beverage manufacturers, and big grocery retailers for 18 months, or until Congress passed broader legislation on food-industry concentration. It would also have created a 12-member commission to study how concentrated the food and farm economy has become, from seed sellers to meatpackers to supermarkets, and recommend changes to antitrust law. The Attorney General could waive the merger freeze only in extraordinary cases, like a company's insolvency.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers facing a handful of dominant buyers, rural communities that depend on farm income, food shoppers whose grocery prices have not fallen along with farm prices, and food-chain workers in concentrated industries. Farmers' organizations and rural advocates backed the approach.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Family farmers, rural communities, grocery shoppers

how_it_helps.text: The bill cites government figures that the top 4 beef packers went from 32% to 85% market share and top 4 pork packers from 36% to 71% over three decades, leaving farmers selling into markets with one or two realistic buyers in their region [S3].
It notes that farmers now keep roughly 15 cents of every retail food dollar, down from 41 cents in 1950, while net farm income has fallen by more than half since 2013 [S3].
By freezing large mergers for 18 months, the bill would have stopped further consolidation of meat processing, seed, grain, and grocery businesses while Congress considered broader fixes [S3].

The commission would have had to study why low farm prices have not produced lower supermarket prices, and whether existing antitrust law adequately protects family farms and shoppers, with findings and recommendations due to Congress and the President within 12 months [S3].
The bill directs that at least four of the commission's hearings be held in different agriculture regions of the country, not only in Washington [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large agribusiness firms, meatpackers, seed and agrichemical companies, food and beverage manufacturers, and big grocery chains would have lost the ability to buy rivals during the freeze, and would have faced a federal review of their market power. Some merger activity that could have produced efficiencies or rescued failing firms would have been blocked.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large agribusinesses, meatpackers, seed firms, grocery chains

drawbacks.text: An across-the-board moratorium is a blunt instrument: it would block all qualifying mergers for 18 months, including deals that might have created real efficiencies or rescued a financially distressed company, unless the Attorney General granted a waiver for extraordinary circumstances such as insolvency [S3].

The moratorium runs only 18 months unless Congress enacts comprehensive legislation, and the study commission makes recommendations only, so the bill by itself would not lower any prices or restore any competition; its main product is a report [S3].

Critics of antitrust intervention in agriculture argue that consolidation reflects scale economies in processing and distribution, and that blocking mergers could raise costs that are passed to consumers; the bill text does not address these objections beyond asserting that concentration harms farmers and shoppers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a pause, not a cure: an 18-month merger freeze plus a $2 million study commission, modest relative to the concentration it describes. Its main value was stopping further consolidation while Congress learned the facts. The main cost is that a blunt moratorium would also block some mergers that might have benefited companies, workers, or shoppers, and the bill offered no exemption process beyond an insolvency waiver. Reasonable people could disagree about the freeze, but the study commission's questions — why grocery prices don't fall when farm prices do, whether antitrust law protects family farms — were ones the industry had little incentive to see answered.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Agriculture and Judiciary committees the day it was introduced and neither committee acted on it, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on September 13, 2018, joined by five original cosponsors including Reps. Pingree, Kaptur, Khanna, DeLauro, and Ellison [S3].
The same day, the House referred it to the Agriculture Committee and, for relevant provisions, to the Judiciary Committee [S1].
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill; all sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats [S4].
The bill's recorded action history ends with the committee referrals — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote is listed — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large agribusiness, meatpackers, seed and agrichemical companies, and grocery chains kept the freedom to merge and acquire through the 2018-2019 consolidation wave, with no freeze and no commission examining their market power. Farmers and shoppers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large agribusinesses kept merging; no freeze or review

sides.party_line_note: All nine initial supporters were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored and the House never voted on the bill, so opposition is visible only in the bill dying in committee without action [S3][S4][S1].

industries.industry: Meat and poultry packers and processors
industries.note: The bill cites top-4 market shares of 85% in beef and 71% in pork and would have frozen large mergers in this sector, whose dominant buyers set prices paid to farmers. Packermen benefit from consolidation, which raises the cost of food margins paid by consumers and farmers alike.

Three firms control roughly two-thirds of the world's commodity crop seed and about 70% of agrichemicals, per the bill's findings; a merger freeze and antitrust review threatened further consolidation. Farmers' seed costs nearly quadrupled over two decades as concentration rose.

Large manufacturers above the bill's size thresholds would have been barred from acquiring rivals during the moratorium, limiting their ability to consolidate further and expand market power over suppliers.

Big retail chains were included in the merger freeze; the bill specifically questions why low farm prices have not translated into lower supermarket prices, a gap that concentrated retail can help maintain.

As sellers into markets dominated by a few buyers, farmers would gain bargaining power from any reversal of consolidation; the bill was framed entirely around their interests and those of rural communities.
